procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders of the courts below annulling the usufructuary mortgage bond in question
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court dealt with the appeal, noting that the Government Advocate conceded the committing court had not complied with certain provisions, but argued the omission was insufficient to overturn the conviction.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court heard the appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 48 of 1957) and the appellant is Narayan Rao. The Supreme Court set aside the orders of the courts below annulling the usufructuary mortgage bond in question and held the transaction binding on the estate of the insolvents. The appeal was allowed.

directions: The orders of the courts below annulling the usufructuary mortgage bond in question are set aside.
The transaction is held binding on the estate of the insolvents.
The lease back to the mortgagors being a part of the same transaction is equally binding on the estate of the insolvents.
The appellant is entitled to his costs throughout, to come out of the estate in the hands of the Official Receiver who must pay his own costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the failure to furnish the accused with copies of documents as required by Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is an illegality that vitiates the trial, or an irregularity curable under Section 537 of the Code.

facts: An accused person was charged with murder under s. 302 of the Indian Penal Code.

The police officer and the inquiring magistrate failed to furnish the accused with copies of documents as required by Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure during the initial proceedings.
The accused did receive the necessary copies in the Sessions Court before the prosecution witnesses were examined.
The accused did not complain about the delay, make a grievance that the time was too short, or request an adjournment at the trial stage.
The issue of non-compliance was raised for the first time on appeal after the accused was convicted and sentenced.
law: The word 'shall' in Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code is interpreted as directory, not mandatory. This means non-compliance does not automatically nullify the proceedings.

A distinction is made between an 'illegality' (a trial conducted in a manner fundamentally different from the Code, which vitiates the trial) and an 'irregularity' (a procedural error in a substantially correct trial).
The failure to furnish documents is considered an irregularity, not an illegality.
An irregularity is curable under Section 537 of the Code unless the accused can demonstrate that the error has caused prejudice to their defense.
application: The Court determined that the appellant's counsel did not even attempt to argue that the accused had been prejudiced by the non-compliance.
Instead, the appellant argued that the omission was an illegality that automatically vitiated the entire trial, irrespective of prejudice. The Court rejected this argument.
The Court noted that since the accused received the copies before the witnesses testified in the Sessions Court, they had the opportunity to prepare their defense and cross-examination.
The fact that the accused made no complaint or request for adjournment at the trial indicated that they were not handicapped in their defense.
Therefore, the Court found that the accused had failed to show any prejudice resulting from the procedural irregularity.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the failure to furnish the accused with copies of documents as required by the Code was a mere irregularity, not an illegality that would automatically vitiate the trial. Since the accused could not show that this omission caused any prejudice to their defense, the irregularity was curable under Section 537 of the Code, and the conviction was upheld.

issue.issue_text: Whether the provisions of Section 173(4) and Section 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure are mandatory or merely directory in nature.

facts: The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death.

During the preliminary inquiry, the police officer and the committing magistrate failed to furnish the appellant with all the necessary documents as required by Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The appellant did not raise this issue during the inquiry or the trial; it was raised for the first time on appeal to the High Court.

The High Court found that the accused had received the necessary copies in the Sessions Court before the witnesses were examined and had not shown any prejudice from the initial failure to provide them.
Before the Supreme Court, the appellant argued that the failure to provide the documents automatically rendered the entire trial null and void, regardless of whether it caused any prejudice.
law: Section 173(4) and Section 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure use the word "shall" in describing the duty of the police and the magistrate to furnish the accused with copies of documents the prosecution intends to rely on.

The interpretation of the word "shall" in a statute can be either mandatory (meaning strict compliance is required, and failure to comply invalidates the action) or directory (meaning non-compliance is an irregularity that does not automatically invalidate the action).
Section 537 of the Code states that a finding, sentence, or order shall not be reversed on account of any error, omission, or irregularity unless a failure of justice has been occasioned.
application: The Court acknowledged that the purpose of these provisions is to safeguard the interests of the accused by ensuring they have all the necessary information to conduct their defense.

However, the Court reasoned that treating these provisions as mandatory would have the "far-reaching effect" of rendering entire proceedings and trials "wholly ineffective." This would lead to reopening long-concluded cases, which would not be conducive to expeditious justice.
Based on this reasoning, the Court held that the word "shall" in both sections is not mandatory but only directory.

The Court established that non-compliance with these provisions is an irregularity that does not invalidate the proceedings unless the accused can show that the omission caused prejudice to their defense.
If no prejudice is shown, the omission is considered a mere irregularity that is curable under Section 537 of the Code.

In this specific case, the appellant made no attempt to demonstrate any prejudice. The documents were eventually supplied, and no grievance was raised at the trial stage about having insufficient time to prepare.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the provisions of Section 173(4) and Section 207A(3) are directory, not mandatory. Therefore, a failure to comply with them does not automatically vitiate the trial. The proceedings are only invalidated if the accused can show that the omission caused prejudice to their defense. Since no prejudice was shown in this case, the non-compliance was a curable irregularity, and the court rejected the argument.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the failure to furnish the accused with copies of documents as required by Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is an illegality that vitiates the trial, or an irregularity curable under Section 537 of the Code.
appellant_arguments: The omission to furnish copies is an illegality that has the effect of vitiating the entire proceedings and the trial.
This omission renders the proceedings null and void, and a fresh trial is necessary ipso facto, irrespective of whether the accused has shown any prejudice.
respondent_arguments: The omission to furnish copies is not sufficient to vitiate the trial unless the accused can show they were prejudiced in their defence.
The omission is a mere irregularity that is curable under Section 537 of the Code.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the provisions of Section 173(4) and Section 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure are mandatory or merely directory in nature.
appellant_arguments: The provisions are mandatory, as evidenced by the argument that non-compliance automatically vitiates the trial without any need to show prejudice.
respondent_arguments: The provisions are directory, as the effect of non-compliance is not automatic but depends on whether prejudice was caused to the accused.

cases.principle: Non-compliance with the provisions of Section 360 of the Code was a mere irregularity that could be cured by the provisions of Section 537.

cases.case_name: Pulukuri Kotayya and others v. King-Emperor
cases.principle: The court adopted the reasoning from this case as a 'complete answer' to the argument that a breach of a statutory provision (Section 162 of the Code) would vitiate the proceedings.

cases.case_name: Gurbachan Singh v. The State of Punjab
cases.principle: To support its conclusion that non-compliance with the provisions of the Code is a curable irregularity, noting that the Court in this case was 'inclined to take a similar view'.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Non-compliance with the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which require furnishing documents to the accused, is a curable irregularity and does not automatically vitiate the proceedings. The word 'shall' in these provisions is directory, not mandatory. The proceedings will only be invalidated if the accused demonstrates that the omission has caused actual prejudice to their defense.
obiter: Magistrates have a duty to be circumspect and ensure that the provisions for supplying necessary documents to the accused are fully complied with so that the accused are not handicapped in their defense.
The distinction between an illegality and an irregularity is one of degree rather than of kind.

If a trial is conducted in a manner substantially prescribed by the Code, an irregularity can be cured under section 537; however, if the trial is conducted in a manner fundamentally different from that prescribed, it is bad and cannot be cured.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The failure to furnish an accused with copies of documents as required by Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not an illegality that automatically vitiates the trial. The word "shall" in these provisions is directory, not mandatory. Such an omission is a curable irregularity under Section 537 of the Code, and will only warrant reopening the proceedings if the accused can demonstrate that the non-compliance caused them prejudice in their defence.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the omission to furnish documents caused prejudice to the accused in their defence. If no prejudice is shown, the omission is a mere irregularity curable under Section 537 of the Code.
why_appellant_lost: The court held that the word 'shall' in Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) is not mandatory but only directory, meaning non-compliance does not automatically vitiate the proceedings.
The appellant failed to demonstrate any prejudice caused by the omission, having not even raised the grievance during the committal proceedings or at trial, but only for the first time on appeal.

The court rejected the argument that the omission was an illegality that rendered the proceedings null and void, finding it should not have a more far-reaching effect than non-compliance with other procedural sections like s. 162 or s. 360, which precedent has established are curable irregularities.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the omission was a mere irregularity curable by reference to Section 537 of the Code, as no case of prejudice had been made out.
The court's reasoning aligned with the respondent's position that the omission was not sufficient to vitiate the trial unless the accused could show they were prejudiced in their defence.
The court adopted the reasoning from precedents like Pulukuri Kotayya v. King-Emperor, which treated breaches of statutory provisions as curable irregularities unless they caused prejudice.
policy_considerations: An omission by a police officer to fully comply with the provisions of s. 173, should not be allowed to have such a far-reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective.

The result contended for by the appellant would necessarily result in re-opening proceedings and trials which may have been concluded long ago, which would be neither conducive to expeditious justice nor in the interest of accused persons themselves.
Accepting the appellant's argument would frustrate the intent of the amending Act, which was to simplify procedure, not complicate it.
